title: Undefeated HSFB HC Resigns After 53-Second Roster Error DQs Team from Playoffs – Bleacher Report
body:
The Middletown High School football program is in turmoil after head coach Tim Strenfel resigned Thursday, following the team's abrupt removal from the New York State Section II playoffs. Officials determined that the Rams had fielded an ineligible player in the opening round of the postseason—a mistake that stemmed from a 53‑second clerical oversight on the roster submission. The error not only cost the undefeated squad a chance at a state title but also raised questions about compliance procedures across high‑school athletics in the region.

Strenfel, who guided the Rams to a perfect 13‑0 regular‑season record and a Section II championship, announced his departure in a brief statement to the school district. “I take full responsibility for the oversight that led to the disqualification,” he wrote, adding that he believed stepping down was in the best interest of the program and its student‑athletes. The resignation comes as the district prepares to appoint an interim coach for the remainder of the season and to conduct an internal review of its eligibility verification processes.

The infraction involved a senior wide receiver who had transferred from a neighboring district earlier in the year. While the player met academic requirements, the transfer paperwork was not finalized by the state’s deadline, rendering him ineligible for postseason play. The oversight was discovered during a routine audit by the Section II officials, who notified the school just hours before the first playoff game. With the clock ticking, the administration was forced to withdraw the team rather than risk further sanctions. The decision sparked immediate backlash from parents, alumni, and community members, many of whom had rallied behind the Rams’ historic run.

Experts in high‑school sports governance note that such roster errors, though rare, underscore the complex web of regulations that schools must navigate. “Eligibility rules are designed to ensure fair competition, but they also place a heavy administrative burden on coaches and athletic directors,” said Dr. Melissa Hargrove, a professor of sports management at SUNY Binghamton. “A single missed deadline can have cascading effects, as we saw here, affecting not just a single player but an entire team’s season.” Hargrove added that the incident could prompt the New York State Public High School Athletic Association (NYSPHSAA) to revisit its verification timeline and provide clearer guidance to schools with high turnover rates.

The fallout extends beyond the football field. Middletown High School’s athletic department is now under scrutiny for its internal checks and balances. District officials have pledged to implement a more robust compliance system, including a dedicated eligibility officer and automated alerts for upcoming deadlines. Meanwhile, the players—many of whom have already secured college scholarships—are left to process the disappointment of a lost opportunity to showcase their talents on a larger stage. Team captain Jordan Miller, who posted a heartfelt video on social media, expressed gratitude for the support of his teammates and vowed to “carry the lessons learned into the next chapter of our lives.”

Looking ahead, the Rams will regroup under an interim coach as they finish the regular season, while the district prepares for a comprehensive audit of its athletic compliance procedures. The incident serves as a cautionary tale for high‑school programs nationwide: meticulous attention to administrative detail is as critical to success as on‑field performance. As the community rallies around its young athletes, the hope is that the lessons learned will strengthen the program’s foundation, ensuring that future seasons are defined by victories earned on the field rather than lost in paperwork.
